name: Antilogic
third_party: The audience, who judge which logos prevails.
ends_well_when: The stronger speech wins the room.
typical_failure: Cleverness detached from any care for truth.
summary: Protagoras was reported to be the first to say that on every matter there are two logoi opposed to each other. Antilogic is the drill that follows: argue the case, then argue its contrary with equal force. Its premise is the homo-mensura doctrine. If each person is the measure, then disagreement is not a defect to be cured but the normal condition of speech, and the trained speaker learns to make the weaker logos the stronger.

name: Eristic
when: late 5th c. BCE; satirised c. 380 BCE
who: Euthydemus and Dionysodorus (as Plato portrays them)
ends_well_when: The opponent is reduced to silence or contradiction.
typical_failure: Victory proves nothing; the question is never addressed.
summary: Argument for the sake of winning. Any answer the respondent gives is turned into a refutation by equivocation, ambiguity or sheer pace. In the Euthydemus the brothers show that a learner both knows and does not know. Aristotle’s Sophistical Refutations is in effect a field guide to eristic, written so that the dialectician can detect and defuse it.

name: Socratic elenchus
third_party: None; bystanders sometimes, but the exchange is dyadic.
ends_well_when: The answerer admits aporia and resolves to inquire further.
typical_failure: Humiliation hardens the answerer instead of freeing them (Callicles, Thrasymachus).
summary: The interlocutor states a thesis, usually a definition of a virtue. Socrates secures assent to further premises the interlocutor holds, then shows that these entail the thesis’s negation. The outcome is aporia, a stalled certainty. Vlastos’s ‘problem of the elenchus’ asks how exposing inconsistency could ever establish truth; the dialogues answer obliquely that what is examined is the person, not only the proposition.

name: Platonic dialectic
third_party: None; the dialectician’s own vision of the forms.
ends_well_when: Sight of the first principle; correct division of kinds.
typical_failure: Closure: the philosopher who has seen the Good stops listening.
summary: In the middle and late dialogues, dialectic becomes the capstone discipline. It runs by hypothesis upward to an unhypothetical first principle, and by collection and division: gather scattered instances under one form, then cut that form ‘at its natural joints’. Disagreement here is a symptom of failure to see the forms. The Republic bars dialectic to the young, who use argument like puppies tearing at whatever is near.

name: Aristotelian dialectic
third_party: Sometimes an examiner or audience in the Academy’s exercises.
ends_well_when: The thesis survives examination, or the answerer is driven to contradiction.
typical_failure: Argument from opinion never touches the world.
summary: A rule-governed game between questioner and answerer, reasoning from endoxa: what is accepted by all, by most, or by the wise. The Topics catalogues the places (topoi) from which arguments may be drawn. Aristotle names three uses: intellectual exercise, encounters with ordinary people, and the philosophical sciences, where working through difficulties on both sides helps one see truth and falsity more easily.

name: Deliberative rhetoric
third_party: The assembly or jury, who decide.
ends_well_when: A decision by the audience.
typical_failure: Demagogy: emotion outruns judgment.
summary: Rhetoric is the counterpart (antistrophos) of dialectic. It finds the available means of persuasion in matters that admit of being otherwise. In its deliberative genre an assembly is persuaded about future advantage. Disagreement is ordinary practical uncertainty, worked through by appeals of ēthos, pathos and logos before a crowd that cannot follow long chains of argument.

name: Stasis theory
when: Hermagoras of Temnos, mid-2nd c. BCE
third_party: Judge or court, whose jurisdiction is itself one of the stases.
ends_well_when: The issue is located; the case is argued at the right stasis.
typical_failure: Assumes a shared forum and law within which the issue can be placed.
summary: A procedure for finding where a dispute actually stands, the point at which the parties come to rest against each other. It asks four questions in order. Conjecture asks whether a thing was done. Definition asks what it should be called. Quality asks whether it was justified. Translation asks whether this forum has jurisdiction. Stasis theory is the oldest explicit taxonomy of what a disagreement is ‘really about’, and it already distinguishes the epistemic, the linguistic, the evaluative and the jurisdictional.

name: Arguing both sides
when: Arcesilaus c. 265 BCE; Carneades in Rome, 155 BCE
third_party: None, or a pupil learning the method.
ends_well_when: Assent to the most persuasive, held provisionally.
typical_failure: Moral corrosion: arguing against justice weakens it.
summary: The sceptical Academy turned Socratic questioning into a standing practice of arguing for and against any thesis. On the Athenian embassy of 155 BCE Carneades argued for justice one day and against it the next, scandalising Cato. Cicero, who admired the method, said it suits the search for what is most probable and trains the orator in copiousness.

name: Pyrrhonian equipollence
when: Pyrrho c. 300 BCE; Aenesidemus 1st c. BCE; Sextus c. 200 CE
ends_well_when: Suspension of judgment, and with it tranquillity.
typical_failure: Practical paralysis, or covert dogmatism about suspension itself.
summary: Scepticism is ‘an ability to set out oppositions among things that appear and are thought of in any way at all’. Equal force on both sides yields suspension of judgment, and tranquillity follows ‘like a shadow’. Disagreement itself (diaphōnia) is the first of Agrippa’s five modes. Undecidable dispute among philosophers and ordinary people is a reason to suspend judgment, not to pick a side.

name: Refusing dispute
when: among the oldest strata of the Pāli canon
who: The Buddha of the Aṭṭhakavagga (Sutta Nipāta, ch. 4)
ends_well_when: The sage does not take the dispute up.
typical_failure: Error goes unchallenged; quietism.
summary: The sage does not enter disputes. Those who say ‘only this is pure’ and call the other a fool are bound by their views (diṭṭhi), and their debates yield only praise or blame and the anxiety of losing. Quarrels arise from what is held dear, and what is held dear from desire. Gómez reads this as a proto-Madhyamaka strand, a therapy of views rather than a better view.

name: Abhidharma controversy
when: trad. Third Council, c. 250 BCE; compiled over centuries
third_party: The orthodox community that preserves the record.
ends_well_when: The dissenting thesis is shown self-contradictory.
typical_failure: The opponent never speaks in their own voice.
summary: A canonical text of over two hundred points of controversy between the Theravāda and rival schools, set out as formalised exchanges. The orthodox questioner extracts an admission, then shows that it entails a contradiction with another admission. It is an early Indian dialogue-logic, structurally close to elenchus but used to police doctrinal boundaries.

name: Vāda (good-faith debate)
third_party: Sometimes judges or a moderator (madhyastha) in public debate.
ends_well_when: The thesis is established or refuted by pramāṇa.
typical_failure: Agreement on the means of knowledge is assumed, not argued.
summary: The Nyāya-sūtra defines vāda as debate between parties who use the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) and the five-membered syllogism to establish or refute, without departing from an accepted doctrine. It is debate among teacher, pupil and peer, aimed at truth. The Caraka-saṃhitā likewise separates friendly discussion (sandhāya sambhāṣā) from hostile disputation and gives etiquette for each.

name: Jalpa & vitaṇḍā
third_party: Judges and audience in public debate.
ends_well_when: One side commits a point of defeat.
typical_failure: Tricks win; truth loses.
summary: Jalpa is debate for victory, permitted to use quibbles (chala), futile rejoinders (jāti) and the opponent’s slips. Vitaṇḍā is jalpa without a counter-thesis: pure refutation. Nyāya permits both, as a hedge of thorns protecting the seedling of truth against unscrupulous opponents. This is a sober admission that good-faith procedures need a defence against bad faith.

name: Prasaṅga (reductio without thesis)
ends_well_when: Every view is shown untenable; grasping ceases.
typical_failure: Looks like nihilism or pure destructive cavil.
summary: The Mādhyamika shows that each of the opponent’s positions entails absurdity, without advancing a position of its own. Pressed by Nyāya critics, Nāgārjuna answers: ‘If I had any thesis, that fault would apply to me. But I do not have any thesis.’ Formally this resembles vitaṇḍā. Its purpose is soteriological, the ‘pacification of conceptual proliferation’ (prapañcopaśama).

name: Syādvāda (sevenfold predication)
when: anekānta early; saptabhaṅgī systematised c. 5th–8th c. CE
ends_well_when: Each claim is indexed to its standpoint; the ‘only’ is dropped.
typical_failure: Everything becomes partly true; no position can be wrong.
summary: Reality is many-sided (anekānta), so every assertion holds only ‘in some respect’ (syāt). The sevenfold scheme combines ‘is’, ‘is not’ and ‘is inexpressible’ under different standpoints (naya). Rival doctrines are recast as partial truths, each valid from its standpoint and false when absolutised. This is the elephant parable formalised as a logic.

name: Tibetan monastic debate
when: Sangphu, 12th c.; Geluk curriculum to the present
who: Chapa Chökyi Senge; Geluk monasteries (Sera, Drepung, Ganden)
third_party: Assembled monks and the abbot, who watch and judge.
ends_well_when: The defender holds the line or is forced to accept an absurd consequence.
typical_failure: Virtuosity in defending a fixed curriculum, not inquiry.
summary: A standing defender sits, and a challenger stands, claps and stamps on each point. The challenger presses consequences (thal ’gyur) built from the defender’s own answers. The defender may reply only ‘I accept’, ‘the reason is not established’ or ‘there is no pervasion’. Dreyfus describes it as hermeneutics through combat: a pedagogy of internalising a canon by being forced to defend it in public.

name: Mohist disputation
third_party: None required: the fit of name to thing decides.
ends_well_when: One side is shown to fit (dang).
typical_failure: Disputes over indexical ‘this’ and ‘that’ do not resolve by fit.
summary: Canon A74: ‘disputation is contending over converse claims’. One party says ‘it is an ox’ and the other ‘it is not’, and only one can fit (dang). Bian is a practice of distinguishing (bian 辨). It asks whether a name fits a thing, and it uses analogical procedures such as ‘parallelising’ (mou) and ‘inferring’ (tui). The Mohists rejected Zhuangzi-style relativism: someone wins every genuine dispute.

name: Rectification of names
when: Analects (5th c. BCE); Xunzi ch. 22 (3rd c. BCE)
ends_well_when: Names are settled; disputes cease.
typical_failure: Semantics by decree.
summary: ‘If names are not correct, speech will not accord with things’ (Analects 13.3). For Xunzi, disordered names breed disordered disputes. The cure is a sage-king who fixes names by convention, after which the people need not dispute. Disagreement is diagnosed as a semantic disorder with a political remedy.

name: Walking two roads
native: 兩行 liǎngxíng; 以明 yǐmíng
third_party: None; there is no neutral judge.
ends_well_when: Both sides allowed to proceed; the sage rests at the hinge.
typical_failure: Detachment that cannot act or decide.
summary: Suppose you and I argue and you beat me: does that make you right? No third party can adjudicate, since any judge either agrees with one of us or with neither. The sage stops at the pivot of the Way (daoshu), lets ‘this’ and ‘that’ both proceed, and uses the light (yiming) of seeing that each ‘this’ is someone else’s ‘that’. This is a mockery of Mohist bian that is also a technique.

name: Court policy debate
who: Han court officials vs. Confucian ‘worthies and literati’
third_party: The throne, which hears and decides.
ends_well_when: Policy decided by the sovereign.
typical_failure: The record is a partisan reworking.
summary: An imperial conference on the state monopolies of salt and iron, written up by Huan Kuan as a set-piece dialogue. On one side stood fiscal statecraft and frontier defence. On the other stood agrarian virtue and the Confucian distrust of profit. It is an early documented instance of structured policy debate between institutional factions before a sovereign arbiter.

name: Dispute for the sake of Heaven
native: מחלוקת לשם שמים machloket l’shem shamayim
when: Hillel & Shammai 1st c. BCE; Mishnah c. 200 CE; Bavli c. 500–600
third_party: The court and the majority, which decide practice without erasing the minority.
ends_well_when: A ruling for practice; all views preserved for study.
typical_failure: Dispute for victory masquerading as dispute for Heaven (Korah).
summary: Avot 5:17: a dispute for the sake of Heaven will endure, and the model is Hillel and Shammai. A dispute not for Heaven’s sake will not endure, and the model is Korah. The Mishnah records the minority view (Eduyot 1:5) so that a later court may rely on it. In Eruvin 13b a heavenly voice declares ‘these and these are the words of the living God’, yet the law follows Hillel, because his school was gentle and taught Shammai’s view first. In the oven of Akhnai (Bava Metzia 59b) the majority overrules a heavenly voice: ‘it is not in heaven’.

name: Havruta
third_party: The text, and behind it the teacher.
ends_well_when: A reading both partners can defend.
typical_failure: Cleverness for its own sake (pilpul).
summary: Two learners argue their way through a text aloud. ‘As iron sharpens iron, so two scholars sharpen one another’ (Taanit 7a). ‘Either companionship or death’ (Taanit 23a). Holzer and Kent analyse it as three paired practices: listening and articulating, wondering and focusing, supporting and challenging. The disagreement is aimed at the text more than at the partner.

name: Jadal & munāẓara
who: Jurists and theologians; Ibn ʿAqīl; Shams al-Dīn al-Samarqandī
third_party: The patron’s majlis or the madrasa audience.
ends_well_when: The claimant’s proof stands or falls under the permitted objections.
typical_failure: Display, envy and rivalry.
summary: Juridical dialectic (jadal) structured legal reasoning in the madrasa through question and objection. Samarqandī’s ‘etiquette of inquiry and disputation’ later recast it as a general theory with fixed roles: claimant, questioner, and the permitted objections (manʿ, naqḍ, muʿāraḍa). The famous majlis of 932 between al-Sīrāfī and Abū Bishr Mattā was itself a dispute about what disputes are about: universal logic, or the grammar of a particular language.

name: Science of juristic disagreement
ends_well_when: The disagreement is explained, not ended.
typical_failure: Legitimised plurality becomes cover for arbitrary choice.
summary: Juristic disagreement is catalogued and explained rather than eliminated. The hadith of ijtihād holds that a judge who strives and is right earns two rewards, and one who strives and errs still earns one. Ibn Rushd’s handbook traces each disagreement to its cause: an ambiguous term, conflicting reports, an analogy pulling against a text. The genre is in effect an ancient account of the burdens of judgment.

name: Scholastic disputation
who: Abelard; Aquinas; the Paris and Oxford faculties
ends_well_when: A determination that answers every objection.
typical_failure: Endless distinctions; questions nobody needs answered.
summary: Abelard’s Sic et Non set authorities against one another, and its prologue gives rules for reconciling them: check the text, the context, and above all the senses of words. The university disputation institutionalised this. The opponens objects, the respondens answers, and the master determines. Every article of the Summa keeps the trace: objections (videtur quod), counter-authority (sed contra), response (respondeo), and replies, often by distinguo.

name: Obligational disputation
who: Walter Burley; Roger Swyneshed; William of Ockham
third_party: A master who sets the positum.
ends_well_when: The respondent survives the time limit without contradiction.
typical_failure: A game cut off from any real question.
summary: A formal logic game. The respondent is ‘obliged’ to maintain a possibly false proposition (the positum). The opponent then proposes further sentences, which the respondent must grant, deny or doubt so as to keep the set consistent. The respondent loses by contradiction. It is commitment management, and modern scholars read it as an ancestor of belief-revision and dialogue logics.

name: Staged religious disputation
third_party: The sovereign, who sets terms and declares the winner.
ends_well_when: Victory declared by power.
typical_failure: It is not a disputation at all.
summary: Before a king, Jewish scholars were compelled to debate Christian (often convert) disputants on whether the Talmud attests the Messiah’s advent. The outcome was politically fixed before it began. Nahmanides was granted freedom of speech and was later prosecuted for publishing his account. The form of disputation persisted while its content became theatre of domination.

name: Free conversation
ends_well_when: Both minds exercised; pleasure in the encounter.
typical_failure: Ease without conclusion; a gentleman’s game.
summary: Montaigne calls conversation ‘the most fruitful and natural exercise of our mind’. He welcomes contradiction: ‘when someone opposes me, he arouses my attention, not my anger’. What he hates is obstinacy and the scholastic manner that cares more for forms than for truth. Disagreement is pleasurable friction between well-made minds, a model taken up by the salon and the honnête homme.

name: Experimental matter of fact
ends_well_when: An attested matter of fact.
typical_failure: Facts are made by instruments and witnesses that can themselves be disputed.
summary: After civil war over doctrine, natural philosophers moved dispute off contested causes and onto witnessed matters of fact. These were produced by machines such as the air-pump, attested by gentlemen, and reported in a modest style. Shapin and Schaffer show this was as much a political technology as an epistemic one: a way of making disagreement safe by giving it a narrow, public, inspectable object. Hobbes saw it as a recipe for faction.

name: Free and open encounter
ends_well_when: Truth emerges or is re-earned through collision.
typical_failure: The loudest voices dominate the ‘marketplace’.
summary: Milton wrote: ‘Let her and Falsehood grapple; who ever knew Truth put to the worse, in a free and open encounter?’ Mill’s second chapter gives the argument its canonical form. The suppressed opinion may be true. It may hold part of the truth. Even if false, its collision with truth keeps truth from becoming dead dogma. ‘He who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that.’

name: Coffeehouse & public sphere
who: London coffeehouses; Parisian salons; German Tischgesellschaften
ends_well_when: Public opinion formed by argument.
typical_failure: Bracketing of status leaves status intact.
summary: On Habermas’s account, private people came together as a public to argue about matters of common concern. Status was bracketed, at least in principle, and only the argument counted. The penny university and the periodical press formed one circuit. Critics note how much was excluded, but the ideal of rational-critical debate among equals sets the norm for later deliberative theory.

name: Calculemus
ends_well_when: A computation shows who is right.
typical_failure: Most disputes do not formalise.
summary: Leibniz imagined a universal characteristic in which reasoning would be calculation. ‘When there are disputes among persons, we can simply say: let us calculate, without further ado, to see who is right.’ Disagreement would become an arithmetic error, detectable on paper. The dream has never been realised and has never died. It lives on in decision theory, Bayesian epistemology and the double crux.

name: Sovereign arbitration
ends_well_when: The arbiter’s sentence, accepted as if right reason.
typical_failure: The arbiter becomes the most dangerous party.
summary: Since no one’s reason is ‘right reason’ by nature, ‘the parties must by their own accord set up for right reason the reason of some arbitrator or judge’. Without this, dispute degenerates toward war. This is the purest form of a procedural answer: do not resolve the disagreement, transfer its outcome to an authority both sides have pre-committed to obey.

name: Adversarial trial & cross-examination
when: lawyerisation of English criminal trial from the 1730s
ends_well_when: A verdict.
typical_failure: The better-funded advocate wins.
summary: Truth is to emerge from a contest between partisan advocates before a passive judge and lay jury. Wigmore called cross-examination ‘beyond any doubt the greatest legal engine ever invented for the discovery of truth’. Langbein traces how defence counsel entered English felony trials only in the 1730s, and with them the modern theory that partisanship itself is truth-conducive.

name: Parliamentary debate
when: Bill of Rights 1689; codified by Jefferson 1801, May 1844, Robert 1876
who: Westminster; US Congress; Henry M. Robert
third_party: The Speaker or chair, who keeps order but does not decide.
ends_well_when: A division; the majority prevails.
typical_failure: Debate as theatre; decisions made elsewhere.
summary: Rule-governed adversarial deliberation that ends in a division. Motions, amendments, speaking in turn and through the chair, and the ban on imputing motives to members all contain hostility without denying it. The ‘loyal opposition’ (Hobhouse, 1826) formalises disagreement as a permanent and legitimate office. Rules of order are a technology for making a body decide while still divided.

name: Competitive debate
when: London debating societies 1770s; Cambridge Union 1815; Oxford Union 1823; Lincoln–Douglas 1858
who: Debating societies; school and university leagues
ends_well_when: A winner on points.
typical_failure: Training in advocacy without conviction.
summary: Sides are assigned, often by lot, and the speaker argues whatever they are given. Ticketed London debating societies of the 1770s–90s took up questions of politics, religion and the sexes. The Unions trained a governing class. The modern tournament formats (British Parliamentary, policy, Lincoln–Douglas) descend from in utramque partem. They prize advocacy over belief, which is either their virtue or their vice.

name: Sense of the meeting
third_party: The clerk, who discerns and minutes the sense of the meeting.
ends_well_when: Unity, or a recorded stand-aside.
typical_failure: Fails when interests genuinely conflict or shared faith is absent.
summary: No vote is taken. The clerk listens for and minutes the ‘sense of the meeting’, the unity the gathered body discerns under divine guidance. A Friend who disagrees may ‘stand aside’ or may block. Disagreement is read as unfinished discernment, not as opposing interests, and silence is a working instrument. This is the source of most secular consensus process.

name: Palaver & consensus
who: Akan (Asante) councils; West African palaver traditions
ends_well_when: A shared basis for action.
typical_failure: Consensus that silences juniors, women and outsiders.
summary: Wiredu reconstructs Asante council politics as consensual rather than majoritarian. Talk continues until a position is reached that all can accept as a basis for action, though not necessarily one all believe true. The premise is that ultimate interests are shared even when immediate interests conflict. Wiredu offers it as a model for a ‘non-party polity’.

name: Activist consensus process
when: Movement for a New Society 1971; anti-nuclear and Occupy movements
who: Movement for a New Society; Clamshell Alliance; Occupy
ends_well_when: No remaining block.
typical_failure: Hidden elites and exhaustion; the patient minority rules.
summary: Quaker practice secularised for movements. It uses facilitator roles, temperature checks, blocks and stand-asides. Disagreement is treated as information about a proposal’s weakness. Its known pathologies are tyranny of the patient, exhaustion and the hidden veto. These inspired later hybrids (sociocracy’s ‘consent’, ‘no paramount objection’).

name: Speculative dialectic
third_party: None; the movement of the concept itself.
ends_well_when: Sublation into a richer standpoint.
typical_failure: Every opponent is pre-absorbed into the system.
summary: Each shape of consciousness, pressed to its own standard, generates its contradiction and is sublated: cancelled, preserved and raised. Disagreement is the motor of thought and of history. The textbook formula ‘thesis–antithesis–synthesis’ is Fichte’s and Chalybäus’s, not Hegel’s (Mueller 1958). The master–servant section makes the struggle for recognition the primal scene of conflict.

name: Eristic dialectic
ends_well_when: Victory, by whatever stratagem works.
typical_failure: It works, which is the problem.
summary: Schopenhauer gives thirty-eight stratagems ‘for being right’, with the opponent’s ruin as the explicit aim. The diagnosis is moral psychology. If people were honest, every debate would aim at truth. But innate vanity cannot bear to be wrong, so in most cases we argue for victory. The final stratagem, when all else fails, is to become personal.

name: Community of inquiry
third_party: Reality, through the community of investigators.
ends_well_when: Convergence in the long run.
typical_failure: ‘The long run’ may never come for this dispute.
summary: Doubt is an irritation that inquiry relieves. Peirce ranks four ways of fixing belief: tenacity, authority, the a priori method, and science. Only science lets ‘some external permanency’ settle opinion, so that all who investigate will in the long run converge. Disagreement is a temporary state of an unfinished inquiry, and the remedy is more and better-designed inquiry.

name: Integration
ends_well_when: An integration in which both desires find a place.
typical_failure: Not every conflict can be integrated.
summary: Conflict is ‘the appearance of difference, difference of opinions, of interests’, and should be used rather than deplored. There are three ways to deal with it. Domination gives one side its way. Compromise makes each side give up something. Integration finds a solution in which ‘both desires have found a place’. In her library example, one reader wanted the window open and another wanted it shut, and opening a window in the next room satisfied both. Getting to Yes is largely Follett with case studies.

name: Strategic bargaining
who: John Nash; Thomas Schelling; Howard Raiffa
third_party: None, or an arbitrator in some models.
ends_well_when: An equilibrium agreement inside the zone of possible agreement.
typical_failure: Values and identities do not show up as payoffs.
summary: Conflict is a mixed-motive game: the parties share an interest in agreement and differ on its terms. Nash derives a unique bargaining solution from axioms. Schelling shows that commitment, focal points and threats shape outcomes more than arguments do. Raiffa turns this into practical analysis of BATNAs and zones of possible agreement. Disagreement is modelled as payoff structure, not belief.

name: Interactive problem-solving workshop
who: John Burton; Herbert Kelman; John Paul Lederach
third_party: A panel of scholar-practitioners as facilitators.
ends_well_when: Shared analysis and new options carried back home.
typical_failure: Insights do not transfer to official negotiators.
summary: Unofficial representatives of warring communities meet with a panel of social scientists. They analyse the conflict jointly instead of negotiating positions. Burton’s premise, later his human-needs theory, is that deep-rooted conflict stems from non-negotiable needs for identity, security and recognition. These needs, unlike interests, cannot be bargained away and must be satisfied. Lederach widened this into ‘conflict transformation’ of relationships and structures.

name: Restorative justice & circles
who: Howard Zehr; John Braithwaite; Kay Pranis
ends_well_when: Agreement on repair; relationship restored.
typical_failure: Pressure on victims to forgive.
summary: Crime and conflict are reframed as harm to people and relationships, not violation of a rule against the state. Victim, offender and community meet in a facilitated encounter or a talking-piece circle to name the harm, take responsibility and repair. Braithwaite adds ‘reintegrative shaming’: disapproval of the act within continued respect for the person.

name: Mediation
when: Pound Conference 1976; Bush & Folger 1994; Winslade & Monk 2000
who: Frank Sander; Robert Baruch Bush & Joseph Folger; John Winslade & Gerald Monk
third_party: A neutral mediator who controls process, not outcome.
ends_well_when: A voluntary agreement; or, in transformative mode, empowerment and recognition.
typical_failure: Private settlement under power imbalance.
summary: Sander’s ‘multi-door courthouse’ launched modern alternative dispute resolution: send each dispute to the process that fits it. Facilitative mediation seeks interest-based settlement. Transformative mediation drops settlement as the goal and aims at empowerment and recognition, so that each party regains clarity and sees the other. Narrative mediation, drawing on Foucault, helps parties deconstruct ‘conflict-saturated stories’ and co-author alternatives.

name: Principled negotiation
ends_well_when: A wise agreement measured by objective criteria.
typical_failure: Ignores the hard distributive core.
summary: The method has four rules. Separate the people from the problem. Focus on interests, not positions. Invent options for mutual gain. Insist on objective criteria. Know your BATNA. The epistemic core is the claim that positions are lossy encodings of interests, and that interests are more often compatible than positions are.

name: Difficult conversations
who: Douglas Stone; Bruce Patton; Sheila Heen
ends_well_when: Each person understands the three conversations; a way forward.
typical_failure: Treats structural conflict as interpersonal.
summary: Every hard conversation is three conversations at once. The ‘what happened’ conversation is about truth, intent and blame. The feelings conversation is about what each person feels. The identity conversation asks what this says about me: am I competent, good, lovable? Shift from certainty to curiosity, from blame to contribution, from inferred intent to reported impact.

name: Rogerian exchange
third_party: None; or a facilitator enforcing the rule.
ends_well_when: Each side understood to its satisfaction.
typical_failure: Asks the weaker party to accommodate.
summary: Rogers names ‘our very natural tendency to judge, to evaluate’ as the main barrier to communication. His test is that each person may speak up for himself only after he has first restated the ideas and feelings of the previous speaker accurately, and to that speaker’s satisfaction. Rhetoricians turned this into ‘Rogerian argument’: reduce threat, state the opponent’s position fairly, find common ground, then propose.

name: Rapoport’s rules & region of validity
ends_well_when: The opponent feels understood and can hear the rebuttal.
typical_failure: Useless against someone fighting, not debating.
summary: Rapoport distinguishes three kinds of conflict. In fights the aim is to harm the opponent. In games the aim is to outwit them within rules. In debates the aim is to convince them. In a true debate one must reduce the opponent’s sense of threat by showing that one understands their position. One does this by stating the ‘region of validity’ in which their view is correct. Dennett distilled this into four rules: re-express, list agreements, mention what you learned, and only then rebut.

name: Nonviolent Communication
ends_well_when: Needs named and a request accepted.
typical_failure: Scripted empathy; jargon used as a weapon.
summary: Every utterance can be heard as an expression of observation, feeling, need and request. Judgments, demands and diagnoses are ‘tragic expressions of unmet needs’. Needs are universal and never actually in conflict. Strategies are what collide. Disagreement is thus re-described at the level where, by hypothesis, it disappears.

name: Motivational interviewing
ends_well_when: The person voices their own reasons for change.
typical_failure: Steering dressed as neutrality.
summary: Arguing for change produces resistance, because the listener voices the other side of their own ambivalence. MI instead uses reflective listening to evoke the person’s own reasons for change, and it ‘rolls with resistance’. It is a clinical method that has become a general template for persuasion without confrontation, and it is a direct ancestor of street epistemology and deep canvassing.

name: Bohmian dialogue
third_party: Facilitator only at first; then none.
ends_well_when: Shared meaning; thought seen as a collective process.
typical_failure: Endless talk without decision.
summary: A group of about twenty to forty people meets without agenda or decision. Participants practise suspending their assumptions, neither acting on them nor suppressing them, so that the group can observe thought as a collective, self-sustaining process. Disagreement shows where unexamined assumptions defend themselves as if they were the self.

name: Reflective structured dialogue
who: Laura Chasin; Richard Chasin; Margaret Herzig
ends_well_when: Stereotypes broken; complexity visible.
typical_failure: Civility without change.
summary: Family therapists applied systemic techniques to polarised public issues, starting with abortion. Participants agree to communication rules. They answer prepared questions in timed rounds, beginning with personal experience. They are asked to name uncertainties and ‘grey areas’ within their own view. The aim is to break the ‘old conversation’ of stereotyped positions and to make each side’s complexity visible.

name: Street epistemology
ends_well_when: The interlocutor lowers their confidence or examines their method.
typical_failure: Persuasion disguised as inquiry.
summary: This is the elenchus crossed with motivational interviewing. The questioner targets not the belief but the method by which the belief is held, asks for a confidence level, and explores what would change it. It is openly persuasive in intent, though practitioners stress rapport and the interlocutor’s autonomy.

name: Moral reframing
ends_well_when: Measurable increase in support.
typical_failure: Instrumentalises the other’s values.
summary: People argue in the moral foundations of their own side, and so fail to persuade the other. Experiments find that framing a position in the opponent’s moral terms, such as environmentalism framed as purity or a liberal policy framed as patriotism, measurably increases support. This is Aristotle’s audience-adaptation with a psychometric instrument.

name: Deep canvassing
who: Leadership LAB (Los Angeles LGBT Center); David Broockman; Joshua Kalla
ends_well_when: Measurable, durable attitude change.
typical_failure: Effects smaller and less general than hoped.
summary: Canvassers hold ten-minute door-step conversations. They ask for the voter’s view, listen non-judgmentally, exchange personal stories, and invite the voter to reflect on a time they were judged. Field experiments found durable attitude change. An earlier, fabricated study of the method (LaCour & Green, 2014, retracted 2015) makes the later replication more, not less, significant.

name: Toulmin model
ends_well_when: The disagreement located at data, warrant or backing.
typical_failure: Field-dependence leaves cross-field disputes open.
summary: Practical argument is modelled jurisprudentially, not geometrically. A claim rests on data through a warrant, which has backing and is limited by a qualifier and rebuttals. Many disagreements turn out to sit at the warrant, the inference licence, and not at the data or the claim. Warrants are ‘field-dependent’, so disputes across fields need a meta-argument about which warrants govern.

name: Formal dialectic & dialogue types
who: C. L. Hamblin; Douglas Walton; Erik Krabbe
ends_well_when: Commitments made explicit; fallacies flagged.
typical_failure: Idealises away emotion and power.
summary: Hamblin modelled argument as a rule-governed game in which each move updates a participant’s commitment store, and he defined fallacies as illegal moves. Walton and Krabbe classified dialogue by initial situation and goal: persuasion, inquiry, negotiation, deliberation, information-seeking and eristic. A fallacy then often turns out to be a covert shift from one dialogue type to another.

name: Discourse ethics
third_party: None; the ideal community of discourse.
ends_well_when: Consensus under ideal conditions.
typical_failure: Consensus as a hidden demand to speak in one idiom.
summary: Every speech act raises validity claims: truth, normative rightness, sincerity and comprehensibility. When a claim is contested, communication shifts into discourse, where only ‘the unforced force of the better argument’ should count. Norms are valid if all affected could accept them as participants in such discourse. Disagreement is a breakdown in mutual understanding that discourse is designed to repair.

name: Pragma-dialectics
third_party: None; an analyst may reconstruct the discussion.
ends_well_when: Standpoint retracted or doubt withdrawn.
typical_failure: Real arguers are not ideal discussants.
summary: An ideal model of ‘critical discussion’ for resolving a difference of opinion on the merits. It runs through four stages: confrontation, opening, argumentation and concluding. Ten rules govern it, among them the freedom rule, the burden-of-proof rule, the standpoint rule and the closure rule. Each fallacy is a violation of a specific rule at a specific stage. Later work on ‘strategic manoeuvring’ admits that real arguers want both to be reasonable and to win.

name: Deliberative polling
ends_well_when: A measured, considered public opinion.
typical_failure: Deliberation favours the already-fluent.
summary: A random sample of citizens is polled, given balanced briefing materials and competing experts, and deliberates in moderated small groups over a weekend. The sample is then polled again. The output is a counterfactual: what the public would think if it had the chance to think. Disagreement is treated as partly a product of inattention and misinformation, which deliberation reduces, and partly as real and reportable.

name: Agonistic pluralism
ends_well_when: None final; conflict channelled.
typical_failure: No criterion separates adversary from enemy.
summary: Against Habermasian consensus, Mouffe argues that antagonism is ineradicable and every consensus is a hegemonic settlement that excludes. The democratic task is to turn antagonism (enemy against enemy) into agonism (adversary against adversary): opponents who share allegiance to liberty and equality and fight over their interpretation. Disagreement should be given institutional channels, not dissolved.

name: Citizens’ assemblies
who: BC Citizens’ Assembly on Electoral Reform; Irish Citizens’ Assembly
ends_well_when: A recommendation, usually to parliament or referendum.
typical_failure: A small group decides for millions.
summary: A body selected by lot hears evidence, deliberates over weeks or months, and recommends. The Irish Assembly’s recommendation on the Eighth Amendment preceded the 2018 referendum. Gutmann and Thompson supply the normative frame. Moral disagreement is permanent and reasonable, so the rules of deliberation should be reciprocity, publicity and accountability, not the hope of agreement.

name: Bridging systems
who: Colin Megill et al. (Pol.is); Audrey Tang; X/Twitter
ends_well_when: Statements that win support across clusters.
typical_failure: Bridging rewards blandness.
summary: Participants vote agree or disagree on short statements written by one another. Dimensionality reduction maps the opinion clusters, and the system surfaces statements that win support across clusters. Community Notes publishes a fact-check only when raters who usually disagree both rate it helpful. Disagreement is modelled as geometry, and the target is the bridging statement, not the median.

name: AI-mediated deliberation
ends_well_when: A group statement most participants endorse.
typical_failure: Whose common ground? The model’s priors shape it.
summary: A language model drafts group statements from individual opinions, collects critiques, and revises. In UK experiments the AI-mediated statements were preferred over those of human mediators, and they reduced within-group division. This raises an old question in new form: whose ‘common ground’ does the mediator find, and what does it leave out?

name: Adversarial collaboration
third_party: An arbiter who holds the data.
ends_well_when: A jointly agreed result.
typical_failure: Few participants actually change their minds.
summary: Scientists who disagree co-design a study whose outcome each agrees in advance would count against their view. An arbiter holds the data. Kahneman proposed it as an alternative to the ‘angry science’ of comment and reply. It works best when the dispute can be operationalised, and it reveals how often it cannot.

name: Ideological Turing test & steelmanning
ends_well_when: Indistinguishability from a true believer.
typical_failure: Mimicry without understanding.
summary: Can you state your opponent’s view so well that their own side cannot tell you from a true believer? Caplan’s test, taking off from Mill’s ‘know the other side’, operationalises understanding as indistinguishability. Steelmanning asks for the strongest version, which may be stronger than the one its holders actually hold. That subtle difference sometimes turns charity into ventriloquism.

name: Double crux
who: Center for Applied Rationality; Duncan Sabien
ends_well_when: A shared crux identified and investigated.
typical_failure: Value and identity disputes have no crux.
summary: Each party finds their crux, a belief that, if it changed, would change their conclusion. Then they look for a double crux: a single empirical or conceptual question on which both conclusions depend in opposite directions. The dispute is moved down the belief-graph until it reaches something testable. This assumes disagreement is a matter of models and that both parties are trying to be right. Aumann’s theorem stands in the background.
